_meta: Eight A/A tests -- experiments where the two arms are IDENTICAL, so the true effect is zero and any 'significant' result is a false positive -- used to show why PEEKING (repeatedly checking significance as data arrives and stopping at the first significant look) inflates the false-positive rate far above the nominal 0.05. Each trajectory is one A/A test's two-sided z-statistic recorded at five successive interim looks as data accumulates; because the true effect is zero the z-statistic just wanders around 0. z_threshold is the two-sided 0.05 critical value (1.96). A FIXED-HORIZON analyst looks only once, at the final look, and declares significance only if the final |z| >= 1.96 -- this controls the false-positive rate at the nominal level. A PEEKING analyst checks every interim look and stops to declare significance the first time |z| crosses 1.96 -- which happens far more often, because a wandering statistic gets many chances to cross. Here the fixed-horizon rule flags 1 of 8 A/A tests (near the nominal level given the tiny sample), while peeking flags 5 of 8 -- five false positives from the same data, four of them on trajectories that crossed at an interim look and then drifted back below the threshold by the end. z_threshold, true_effect, and trajectories are the fixture; every crossing, stopping point, and false-positive rate is computed. This is an illustrative hand-set sample of size 8, not a large simulation; it shows the mechanism, and the general result (peeking inflates the false-positive rate, worse with more looks) is standard sequential-testing theory.
